title: Inverse Matrices & Properties
description: Matrix arithmetic properties, where the real-number rules break (cancellation & zero-product), matrix polynomials, the inverse of a matrix, the 2x2 inverse formula, and the inverse/transpose theorems (1.4.7-1.4.9)

questions.prompt: Matrix addition is commutative: $A + B = B + A$ for matrices of the same size.
explanations: Entrywise addition of real numbers is commutative, so adding matrices entrywise is too.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition is associative: $(A + B) + C = A + (B + C)$.
explanations: Grouping doesn't matter for entrywise addition, so this always holds.

questions.prompt: For matrices of the same size, $A - B = B - A$ in general.
explanations: Subtraction is not commutative — $A-B$ and $B-A$ are negatives of each other, not equal in general.

questions.prompt: Matrix multiplication is associative: $A(BC) = (AB)C$, whenever the products are defined.
explanations: Regrouping the factors doesn't change the product, as long as the sizes stay compatible.

questions.prompt: Matrix multiplication distributes over addition: $A(B+C) = AB + AC$, whenever the products are defined.
explanations: This distributive law holds on both the left and the right.

questions.prompt: For square matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size, $AB = BA$ is always true.
explanations: Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general — order matters.

questions.prompt: $AI = A$ for any matrix $A$ and identity matrix $I$ of matching size.
explanations: The identity matrix acts like the number 1: multiplying by it changes nothing.

questions.prompt: $IA = 0$ (the zero matrix) for any matrix $A$ and identity matrix $I$ of matching size.
explanations: $IA = A$, not $0$ — the identity matrix leaves $A$ unchanged, it doesn't zero it out.

questions.prompt: $A + 0 = A$ for any matrix $A$ and zero matrix $0$ of matching size.
explanations: The zero matrix acts like the number 0 for addition — adding it changes nothing.

questions.prompt: Because $AB \neq BA$ in general, matrix addition $A+B$ is also not always equal to $B+A$.
explanations: Addition and multiplication are different operations — addition stays commutative even though multiplication isn't.

questions.prompt: If $AB = BA$ happens to hold for one particular pair of matrices $A$ and $B$, it must hold for every pair of square matrices of that size.
explanations: $AB=BA$ can happen for special pairs (like $A=I$) without multiplication being commutative in general.

questions.prompt: $A \cdot 0 = 0$ (the zero matrix) for any matrix $A$ and zero matrix $0$ of matching size.
explanations: Multiplying anything by the zero matrix produces the zero matrix.

questions.prompt: Scalar multiplication distributes over matrix addition. Which identity is correct?
explanations: This forgets to multiply $c$ into $B$ as well.
This confuses scalar distributivity with a multiplication rule — there's no $c(AB)$ identity like this.
This mixes up how scalars combine: $(c+d)A = cA + dA$, not a product.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is generally FALSE for square matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ of the same size?
explanations: This associative law for addition is always true.
This distributive law is always true.
This associative law for multiplication is always true.

questions.prompt: For a square matrix $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ of the same size, which is true?
explanations: Multiplying by the identity never zeroes out a matrix.
$IA$ equals $A$, not $I$, for any matrix $A$.
Multiplying by the identity from either side always gives back $A$.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the identity matrix's role in matrix algebra?
choices: It behaves like the number 0 under multiplication
It has no special multiplicative role
It is only defined for $2\times 2$ matrices
It behaves like the number 1 under multiplication
explanations: That describes the zero matrix's role under addition, not the identity's role.
The identity matrix's whole purpose IS its special multiplicative role.
Identity matrices exist for every size, not just $2\times 2$.

questions.prompt: If $A$, $B$, $C$ are matrices of compatible sizes, $A(BC)$ equals:
explanations: This reorders the factors — matrix multiplication is not commutative, so order matters.
This reorders the factors — not what regrouping does.
This reorders the factors — not what regrouping does.

questions.prompt: Matrix multiplication is _____ in general, even when both $AB$ and $BA$ are defined and the same size.
questions.explanation: Order matters for matrix multiplication: $AB$ and $BA$ can be completely different matrices.

questions.prompt: For any matrix $A$ and the appropriately-sized identity matrix, $AI = IA = $ _____.
questions.explanation: The identity matrix leaves any matrix unchanged under multiplication, from either side.

questions.prompt: How many entries in a $2 \times 2$ identity matrix are equal to 1?
questions.explanation: The identity matrix has 1's only on the main diagonal — a $2\times 2$ identity has two of them.

questions.prompt: If $AB = AC$ and $A \neq 0$, then it must be true that $B = C$.
explanations: Unlike real-number cancellation, this can fail for matrices — there exist nonzero $A$ with $AB=AC$ but $B \neq C$.

questions.prompt: If $AB = 0$ (the zero matrix), then $A = 0$ or $B = 0$ must be true.
explanations: The zero-product property fails for matrices — two nonzero matrices can multiply to give the zero matrix.

questions.prompt: Because matrix multiplication can fail the zero-product property, matrix 'division' is not a well-defined operation in general.
explanations: Without a reliable zero-product property, there's no consistent way to 'undo' multiplication by every matrix.

questions.prompt: For real numbers, if $xy = 0$ then $x=0$ or $y=0$ — but the analogous statement is false for matrices.
explanations: This is exactly the zero-product property failing for matrices, even though it holds for real numbers.

questions.prompt: The real-number cancellation law (if $ax=ay$ and $a \neq 0$, then $x=y$) fails for matrices because:
choices: there exist nonzero matrices $A$ with $AB=AC$ even though $B \neq C$
the zero matrix does not exist
explanations: Non-commutativity is a separate issue from cancellation failing.
Matrices can absolutely be multiplied when sizes are compatible.
The zero matrix exists — it's part of what makes these counterexamples work.

questions.prompt: The failure of the zero-product property for matrices means:
choices: the zero matrix cannot be multiplied
every matrix has a zero product with itself
two nonzero matrices can multiply to give the zero matrix
explanations: The zero matrix can be multiplied like any other matrix.
This isn't generally true for an arbitrary matrix.
Matrices certainly can equal the zero matrix.

questions.prompt: Which statement explains why we cannot simply 'divide both sides by $A$' in a matrix equation $AB = AC$?
choices: division of matrices is defined but rarely used
$A$ might not have an inverse, and even when $A$ IS invertible you must multiply by $A^{-1}$ on the correct side
explanations: Matrices appear in equations constantly — that's not the issue.
That's exactly what can fail — the whole point of this question.
There is no matrix 'division' operation — only multiplication by an inverse.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$. Compute the $(1,1)$ entry of $AB$.
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$. Compute the $(1,2)$ entry of $AC$.
questions.explanation: $(AC)_{12} = 1(1) + 1(1) = 2$ — matching $(AB)_{12}$, which is exactly why $AB=AC$ even though $B \neq C$.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(2,2)$ entry of $AB$?
questions.explanation: $(AB)_{22} = 0(0) + 0(1) = 0$ — in fact $AB$ is the entire zero matrix here.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Then $AB = $ _____, even though neither $A$ nor $B$ is the zero matrix.
questions.explanation: $AB = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ — a nonzero-times-nonzero product that still comes out zero.

questions.prompt: For a square matrix $A$, the expression $A^2 - 3A + 2I$ is a valid matrix expression (with $I$ the identity matrix of matching size).
explanations: $A^2$, $3A$, and $2I$ are all matrices of the same size, so they can be combined by addition and subtraction.

questions.prompt: The expression $A^2 + B$, where $A$ is $2\times 2$ and $B$ is $3\times 3$, is defined.
explanations: $A^2$ is $2\times 2$ while $B$ is $3\times 3$ — matrices must be the same size to add them.

questions.prompt: For a square matrix $A$, $A^2$ means $A$ multiplied by itself: $A^2 = A \cdot A$.
explanations: Matrix powers are defined the same way as for numbers — repeated multiplication by itself.

questions.prompt: In the expression $A^2 - 3A + 2I$ for a square matrix $A$, the term '$2I$' means:
choices: the number 2 added to every entry of $A$
2 times the identity matrix, added entrywise
explanations: That would just be $A + 2$, which is not the same as $2I$.
There is no 'division by a matrix' operation here.
$2I$ is a whole matrix, not a single entry of $A$.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(1,1)$ entry of $A^2$?
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(1,1)$ entry of $A^2 - 3A + 2I$?
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(2,2)$ entry of $A^2 - 3A + 2I$?
If $A$ is invertible, we write its inverse as $A^{-1}$.
explanations: This is standard notation, directly parallel to $a^{-1}$ for real numbers.

questions.prompt: Just as the real number $0$ has no multiplicative inverse, some nonzero square matrices also have no inverse.
explanations: A nonzero square matrix can still fail to be invertible — for example, any matrix with determinant 0.

questions.prompt: Every square matrix has an inverse.
explanations: Only square matrices CAN have inverses — but not every square matrix does. Singular matrices don't.

questions.prompt: Only square matrices can be invertible.
explanations: Invertibility (in the $AB=BA=I$ sense) requires $A$ and $B$ to be square and the same size.

questions.prompt: A matrix that IS invertible is sometimes called 'singular.'
explanations: It's the opposite: an invertible matrix is called 'nonsingular.' 'Singular' means it has NO inverse.

questions.prompt: A square matrix $A$ is called invertible if there exists a matrix $B$ such that:
explanations: That would make $B$ related to a very different property, not an inverse.
Adding to get the identity is not the definition of an inverse.
That would force very special conditions on $B$, not the general definition.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is invertible, its inverse $A^{-1}$ is:
choices: different depending on which side you multiply from
explanations: The inverse works the same from either side: $AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I$.
Any invertible square matrix has an inverse, not just diagonal ones.
$A^{-1} = A$ only in special cases (like $A=I$), not in general.

questions.prompt: Which of these is required for $AB = BA = I$ to define $A^{-1} = B$?
choices: $A$ and $B$ must both be square matrices of the same size
explanations: $A$ can be any invertible square matrix, not just the identity.
Symmetry is not required for a matrix to have an inverse.
$B$ is the inverse of $A$, not equal to $A$, in general.

questions.prompt: The real-number analogy for a matrix inverse is: just as $a \cdot a^{-1} = 1$ for nonzero real numbers, $A \cdot A^{-1} = $ _____ for an invertible matrix $A$.
questions.explanation: The identity matrix $I$ plays the role that $1$ plays for real numbers.

questions.prompt: A matrix that has no inverse is called _____.
questions.explanation: 'Singular' and 'not invertible' mean the same thing — for a $2\times 2$ matrix, it means $\det(A) = 0$.

questions.prompt: Multiplying $A$ by its inverse $A^{-1}$, in either order, always gives the identity matrix $I$.
explanations: That's the defining property of an inverse: $AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I$.

questions.prompt: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$, the $2\times 2$ inverse formula states $A^{-1} = $
explanations: This just reuses the original matrix — the formula swaps and negates entries.
This multiplies by the determinant instead of dividing by it.
This uses $ad+bc$ instead of $ad-bc$ in the denominator.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-3&2\end{bmatrix}$. Compute the $(1,1)$ entry of $A \cdot A^{-1}$.
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-3&2\end{bmatrix}$. Compute the $(1,2)$ entry of $A \cdot A^{-1}$.
Compute $\det(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\3&2\end{bmatrix}$.

explanations: Order flips: the correct formula is $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
This is part of Theorem 1.4.7 — inverses and powers commute in this specific sense.

questions.prompt: Because $(A^n)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^n$, it must also be true that $(A+B)^{-1} = A^{-1}+B^{-1}$.
explanations: The power rule for inverses doesn't extend to sums — in fact $A+B$ might not even be invertible when $A$ and $B$ are, and there is no addition rule for inverses like this.

questions.prompt: Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, we must be careful about order when inverting or transposing a product.
explanations: Both $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$ and $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$ reverse the order — a direct consequence of $AB \neq BA$ in general.
Inverting twice returns the original matrix, not $A^{-1}$ again.
$(A^{-1})^{-1}$ equals $A$ itself, not the identity.
There's no reason inverting twice would square the matrix.

questions.prompt: The correct formula for the inverse of a product is:
explanations: This keeps the original order — but inverting a product reverses the order.
This is just the product again, not its inverse.
Inverses don't combine by addition.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$. What is the $(1,1)$ entry of $(A^{-1})^2$?
Just as the transpose of a product reverses order, the inverse of a product also reverses order: $(AB)^{-1} = $ _____.
questions.explanation: Both the inverse and the transpose of $AB$ come out with the factors in reverse order.

questions.prompt: $(kA)^T = kA^T$ for a scalar $k$.
explanations: Transposing doesn't interact with scalar multiplication — the scalar just comes along for the ride.

questions.prompt: $(A^T)^T = A$ for any matrix $A$.
explanations: Transposing twice undoes itself and returns the original matrix.

questions.prompt: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$, $(AB)^T = A^TB^T$.
explanations: Order matters: $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$, not $A^TB^T$. Computing both sides gives different matrices here.

explanations: Transpose distributes over addition with a plus sign, not a minus.
That formula is for the transpose of a PRODUCT, not a sum.
That's a different combination — not the transpose of a sum.
This keeps the original order — transposing a product reverses the order.
That's the product itself, not its transpose.
That formula is for the transpose of a sum, not a product.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$. Compute the $(1,1)$ entry of $AB$.
$(A+B)C = AC+BC$ for matrices of compatible sizes (the right-distributive law).
explanations: Matrix multiplication distributes over addition on both sides — left and right.

questions.prompt: $c(dA) = (cd)A$ for scalars $c$ and $d$.
explanations: Scalar multiplication is associative — scaling twice by $c$ then $d$ is the same as scaling once by $cd$.

questions.prompt: $-A$ means reversing the order of the rows of $A$.
explanations: $-A$ means negating every entry of $A$ (multiplying by $-1$) — it has nothing to do with row order.

questions.prompt: $A + (-A) = 0$ (the zero matrix), for any matrix $A$.
explanations: Adding a matrix to its negative cancels every entry, giving the zero matrix — just like $x+(-x)=0$.

questions.prompt: The zero matrix and the identity matrix are the same matrix.
explanations: They're different: the zero matrix has all entries $0$, while the identity matrix has $1$'s on the diagonal and $0$'s elsewhere.

questions.prompt: The identity matrix $I$ is the only matrix that satisfies $AI=A$ for every matrix $A$ of compatible size.
explanations: No other matrix has this universal property — that's exactly what makes $I$ the identity.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $p \times q$ with $(m,n) \neq (p,q)$, then $A+B$ is still defined.
explanations: Matrix addition requires both matrices to be exactly the same size — mismatched sizes make $A+B$ undefined.

questions.prompt: Scalar multiplication and matrix multiplication are the same operation.
explanations: They're different operations: scalar multiplication scales every entry by a single number, while matrix multiplication combines two matrices via rows and columns.

questions.prompt: Which property of real-number addition carries over perfectly to matrix addition?
explanations: Associativity carries over too — matrix addition is fully associative.
Commutativity carries over too — matrix addition is fully commutative.
Both properties carry over perfectly for matrix addition.

questions.prompt: The matrix $-A$, added to $A$, gives the _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: $A + (-A) = 0$, the zero matrix — just like $x + (-x) = 0$ for real numbers.

questions.prompt: For matrices, $AB=AC$ does not, on its own, guarantee $B=C$ — even when $A$ is nonzero.
explanations: This is exactly the cancellation law failing — nonzero isn't enough; $A$ also needs to be invertible.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is invertible and $AB=AC$, what can we conclude?
explanations: We can conclude something specific here — they aren't just unrelated.
There's no reason $B$ would be the negative of $C$.
We CAN draw a conclusion: multiplying both sides by $A^{-1}$ gives $B=C$.

questions.prompt: Cancellation ($AB=AC \Rightarrow B=C$) is guaranteed whenever $A$ is invertible.
explanations: Multiplying both sides of $AB=AC$ by $A^{-1}$ on the left gives $B=C$ — this always works when $A^{-1}$ exists.

questions.prompt: The zero-product property (if $AB=0$ then $A=0$ or $B=0$) holds for all square matrices.
explanations: It fails for singular (non-invertible) matrices — two nonzero matrices can multiply to give the zero matrix.

questions.prompt: For matrices, $AB=0$ does NOT imply that $A=0$ or $B=0$ — this is described as the failure of the _____ property.
questions.explanation: The zero-product property holds for real numbers but fails for matrices in general.

questions.prompt: In the expression $A^2 - 3A + 2I$, all three terms must be matrices of the same size for the expression to make sense.
explanations: Addition and subtraction of matrices require matching sizes — $A^2$, $3A$, and $2I$ all have to match.

questions.prompt: A matrix polynomial like $A^2 - 3A + 2I$ can only be formed for a square matrix $A$.
explanations: $A^2 = A \cdot A$ requires $A$ to be square for the product to be defined at all.

questions.prompt: Why must $A$ be square in the expression $A^2 - 3A + 2I$?
choices: Because non-square matrices can't be added
Because $I$ is only defined for square matrices, unlike $A$
There is no requirement that $A$ be square
Because $A^2=A \cdot A$ requires $A$ to be square for the product to be defined
explanations: Addition itself doesn't require square matrices — only matching sizes.
$I$ is always square, but that's not the reason $A$ itself must be square here.
$A$ does have to be square, or $A^2$ wouldn't be defined.

questions.prompt: The expression $A^2 - 3A + 2I$ still makes sense even if $A$ is not square.
explanations: If $A$ isn't square, $A^2=A\cdot A$ isn't even defined, so the whole expression breaks down.

questions.prompt: Two different matrices can each be a valid inverse of the same matrix $A$.
explanations: An inverse, when it exists, is unique — no matrix can have two different inverses.

questions.prompt: If $A$ has an inverse, that inverse must also be a square matrix of the same size as $A$.
explanations: The inverse relation $AB=BA=I$ only type-checks when $A$ and $B$ are square matrices of the same size.

questions.prompt: A non-square matrix can never satisfy $AB=BA=I$ for some matrix $B$.
explanations: If $A$ is $m\times n$ with $m \neq n$, then $AB$ and $BA$ would be different sizes — they could never both equal the same identity matrix.

questions.prompt: An invertible matrix is also called a(n) _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: 'Nonsingular' and 'invertible' mean the same thing.

questions.prompt: If $AB=I$ for square matrices $A$ and $B$, then $A$ and $B$ can never also satisfy $BA=I$.
explanations: For square matrices, this is actually guaranteed to also happen — a one-sided inverse for square matrices is automatically a two-sided inverse.

questions.prompt: $(ABC)^{-1} = C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}$ follows the same order-reversing pattern as $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
explanations: The order-reversing rule extends to any number of invertible factors, not just two.

questions.prompt: The general rule for inverting a product of several matrices is to invert each factor and:
explanations: Keeping the same order gives the wrong formula — the order must reverse.
Inverses of a product don't combine by addition.
Every factor needs to be inverted, not just the first one.

questions.prompt: $(A^{-1})^{-1}=A$ says that inverting a matrix twice returns the original matrix.
explanations: That's exactly what this theorem states — inversion undoes itself.

questions.prompt: $I^{-1}$ does not exist because the identity matrix cannot be inverted.
explanations: The identity matrix is its own inverse: $I \cdot I = I$, so $I^{-1}=I$.

questions.prompt: Inverting a product of matrices reverses their order, the same way _____ a product of matrices reverses their order.
questions.explanation: Both $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$ and $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$ reverse the order of the factors.

questions.prompt: $(A-B)^T = B^T - A^T$ for matrices of the same size.
explanations: The correct formula is $(A-B)^T = A^T - B^T$ — this version has the sign backwards.

questions.prompt: The transpose of a sum equals the sum of the transposes, but the transpose of a product reverses the order of the factors.
explanations: This is exactly the combination of Theorem 1.4.8 (sums) and Theorem 1.4.9 (products).

questions.prompt: Because $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$, we can say the transpose of a product 'reverses the order,' just like the inverse of a product does.
explanations: Both operations share this order-reversing behavior when applied to a product.

questions.prompt: The identity matrix is NOT symmetric: $I^T \neq I$ in general.
explanations: The identity matrix IS symmetric: $I^T = I$, since it's unchanged by swapping rows and columns.

questions.prompt: The zero matrix is symmetric: $0^T = 0$.
explanations: Every entry of the zero matrix is $0$, so swapping rows and columns changes nothing.
